Two different definitions are being contrasted.
A Brønsted acid donates a proton, so it must *contain* an ionisable hydrogen.
A Lewis acid accepts a lone pair, so it must have a vacant orbital.
Check each species.
H₃O⁺ and HCl both have hydrogen to donate, so both are Brønsted acids.
NH₃ has a lone pair to give away, so it is a Lewis **base**, not an acid.
BF₃ has no hydrogen at all, so it can never donate a proton and is not a Brønsted acid. But
boron has only six valence electrons and an empty 2p orbital, so it readily accepts a lone pair:
BF₃ + NH₃ ⇒ F₃B←NH₃
That makes it a Lewis acid and nothing else.
This is exactly why the Lewis definition was needed — it covers electron-pair acceptors such as
BF₃ and AlCl₃ that the proton definition misses entirely.
∴ BF₃.
kcet|Chemistry|2013|39||0|0:
Dry distillation of the calcium salt of a carboxylic acid gives a carbonyl compound, and which
one depends on the salts used.
Two molecules of the **same** salt give a symmetrical ketone:
(CH₃COO)₂Ca ⇒ CH₃COCH₃ + CaCO₃ (acetone)
A calcium salt of formic acid on its own gives an aldehyde with two hydrogens:
(HCOO)₂Ca ⇒ HCHO + CaCO₃ (methanal)
Here the two are distilled **together**, so one acetate group and one formate group combine:
(CH₃COO)Ca(OOCH) ⇒ CH₃CHO + CaCO₃
The methyl comes from the acetate and the hydrogen from the formate, giving ethanal.
This is the general rule: calcium formate mixed with any other calcium carboxylate gives the
corresponding **aldehyde**, because formate contributes the H.
∴ acetaldehyde.
kcet|Chemistry|2013|40||0|0:
Count the orbitals being mixed; the number of hybrid orbitals equals the number of electron
domains, and that fixes the shape.
d²sp³ mixes 2 d + 1 s + 3 p = **six** atomic orbitals, so six equivalent hybrid orbitals are formed.
Six domains arrange themselves as far apart as possible, which puts them at the vertices of an
octahedron, with bond angles of 90°.
For comparison:
sp ⇒ 2 orbitals ⇒ linear, 180°
sp² ⇒ 3 ⇒ trigonal planar, 120°
sp³ ⇒ 4 ⇒ tetrahedral, 109°28′
dsp² ⇒ 4 ⇒ square planar, 90°
sp³d ⇒ 5 ⇒ trigonal bipyramidal
d²sp³ or sp³d² ⇒ 6 ⇒ octahedral
d²sp³ uses inner d orbitals and gives the low-spin octahedral complexes such as [Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺.
∴ an octahedral structure.
kcet|Chemistry|2013|42||0|0:
Acidity of a phenol is decided by how stable the phenoxide ion is after the proton leaves.
An electron-**withdrawing** group pulls the negative charge away and stabilises the anion,
so the phenol is more acidic.
An electron-**releasing** group pushes charge onto the already negative oxygen and
destabilises it, so the phenol is less acidic.
o-Cresol and p-cresol both carry a –CH₃, which releases electrons by induction and
hyperconjugation. Both are therefore **weaker** acids than phenol itself.
p-Nitrophenol carries –NO₂, strongly withdrawing by both −I and −R. From the para position it
can delocalise the negative charge right onto its own oxygen atoms, which is the most effective
stabilisation available here.
The order of acidity is:
cresols < phenol < p-nitrophenol
(pKa about 10.2 for the cresols, 10.0 for phenol, 7.1 for p-nitrophenol.)
∴ p-nitrophenol.
kcet|Chemistry|2013|43||0|0:
A ligand bonds to the central metal by a **coordinate** bond, in which one partner supplies
both electrons. The metal ion has empty orbitals and supplies none, so the ligand must bring
the pair.
Therefore the one indispensable requirement is an unshared (lone) pair of electrons.
Test the other options against real ligands.
(1) Small size is not required — en, EDTA and porphyrins are all large.
(3) A negative charge is not required — NH₃, H₂O and CO are neutral and are among the
commonest ligands of all.
(4) A positive charge actually prevents it. A cation would be repelled by the metal cation, and
in any case it has no spare pair to donate. This is why NH₄⁺ cannot act as a ligand although
NH₃ can — in NH₄⁺ the nitrogen's lone pair is already used up bonding the fourth hydrogen.
∴ only when it has an unshared electron pair.
kcet|Chemistry|2013|45||0|0:
First check the molecular formulae.
Propanone (acetone), CH₃–CO–CH₃ : C₃H₆O
Propanal, CH₃–CH₂–CHO : C₃H₆O
They are the same formula, so they are isomers. Now identify the type.
The functional group differs: acetone has a **ketone** group, with the carbonyl inside the chain,
while propanal has an **aldehyde** group, with the carbonyl at the end.
Isomers with the same formula but different functional groups are **functional isomers**.
(2) Position isomers would keep the same functional group and move it along the chain — that
is propan-1-ol against propan-2-ol.
(3) Geometrical isomerism needs restricted rotation, as across a C=C; there is none here.
(4) Optical isomerism needs a chiral carbon; neither compound has one.
The practical consequence is that they behave quite differently — propanal reduces Tollens'
reagent, acetone does not.
∴ functional isomers.

kcet|Chemistry|2013|47||0|0.s:
By Raoult's law the relative lowering of vapour pressure equals the mole fraction of the solute:
(p° − p)/p° = χsolute = n(solute) / (n(solute) + n(solvent))
The question dissolves 3 g of urea in 45 g of water.
Moles of urea, NH₂CONH₂, molar mass 60:
n = 3/60 = 0.05 mol
Moles of water, molar mass 18:
n = 45/18 = 2.5 mol
χurea = 0.05 / (0.05 + 2.5) = 0.05 / 2.55 = 0.0196
So the relative lowering is about 0.02.
Note the solvent moles belong in the denominator; using 0.05/2.5 alone also gives 0.02 here,
but only because the solution is dilute.
∴ 0.02.

kcet|Chemistry|2013|48||0|0:
Both are aldehydes, so any general carbonyl test will respond to both and cannot distinguish
them. That rules out (3) 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine and (4) semicarbazide, which condense
with every aldehyde and ketone.
Tollens' reagent (1) is also no good here: it oxidises **both** aliphatic and aromatic aldehydes,
so acetaldehyde and benzaldehyde each give a silver mirror.
Fehling's solution is the discriminating one. It is a milder, alkaline Cu²⁺ reagent, and it oxidises
**aliphatic** aldehydes only:
CH₃CHO + 2Cu²⁺ + 5OH⁻ ⇒ CH₃COO⁻ + Cu₂O↓ + 3H₂O
Acetaldehyde gives the characteristic red-brown precipitate of Cu₂O.
Benzaldehyde, being aromatic, does not react — the ring stabilises the aldehyde and the
reagent is not strong enough.
∴ Fehling's solution.
